cards.headline: Own the market, not a guess.
cards.body: An **index fund** holds every company in a {{term:market-index|market index}} at once. Buy a single share and you own a sliver of hundreds of businesses — with no stock-picking required.

art.name: index-basket
art.alt: A single basket holding slices of many companies, representing a whole market index.

cards.headline: One purchase, instant diversification.
cards.body: Because the fund already spans the whole index, a single buy hands you the {{term:diversification|diversification}} that would otherwise take dozens of separate trades to assemble by hand.

cards.headline: ETF or index fund — same core idea.
cards.body: An **ETF** — exchange-traded fund — is an index fund you can buy and sell like a stock through the trading day. Both track a basket; the ETF simply carries a live, changing price.

cards.title: The quiet cost of fees
cards.caption: A fund's {{term:expense-ratio|expense ratio}} is its yearly fee. Two percent sounds tiny, but compounded over decades it quietly claims a large share of your gains.

cards.headline: Fees compound against you.
cards.body: Returns compound in your favor; fees compound against it. The gap between a 0.04% index fund and a 1% active fund can grow into tens of thousands of dollars over a lifetime.

cards.prompt: Two funds track the very same index. One charges 0.04% a year, the other 0.80%. Which should leave more of the market's return in your pocket?

options.label: The 0.80% fund — you get what you pay for

cards.explanation: Holding the same basket, both funds earn the same gross return. The one that skims less off the top leaves more for you. For index funds, low cost **is** the edge.

cards.headline: Most active funds trail the index.
cards.body: Over long stretches, most professional stock-pickers fail to beat their benchmark — especially after fees. That is the whole case for indexing: match the market cheaply instead of paying to try to beat it.

art.name: benchmark-race
art.alt: A steady low-cost index runner pulling ahead of higher-fee active runners in a long race.

cards.body: Three numbers tell you most of what matters about an index fund before you ever buy it.
Since index funds just track a basket, the fee you pay — the [[1]] — is the biggest lever you control.
cards.explanation: You can't control the market's return, but you can control what you pay to capture it. A lower expense ratio is the reliable edge.

cards.summary: An index fund buys the whole market in a single trade — broad, simple, and cheap. Keep costs low and let it compound.
bullets: One purchase gives you a whole index's diversification.
An ETF is the same idea, traded like a stock.
The expense ratio is the fee you most control — keep it low.

art.name: index-basket
art.alt: A basket holding slices of many companies, standing for the whole market owned at once.

cards.insight: You are unlikely to out-pick the market. You can almost always out-save its fees.

sources.title: How Fees and Expenses Affect Your Investment Portfolio
